The radar cross section (RCS) of a chaff cloud is given by the formula σ = 0.172Nλ^2, where N is the number of dipoles and λ is the wavelength of the radar signal.
The four phases of chaff cloud blooming are: 1) Transient phase, 2) Bloom phase, 3) Mature phase, and 4) Decay stage.
Turbulence reduces the blooming time of chaff filaments from 25-50 milliseconds.
The RCS of the turbulent chaff cloud was 1.5-2.5 dBsm higher than the non-turbulent case at 50 milliseconds.
For perpendicular ejection of chaff (90 degrees), the RCS was initially higher than parallel ejection (0 degrees) by 0.1-1 dBsm at 100 milliseconds.
The study used ANSYS Workbench, ANSYS Fluent, and ANSYS HFSS-IE to model and simulate the chaff cloud dynamics and RCS.
The turbulent kinetic energy was varied from 17.5 m^2/s^2 to 18.375 m^2/s^2 by changing the ejection angle of the chaff from parallel (0 degrees) to perpendicular (90 degrees).
The Reynolds numbers ranged from 487,733 × 10^5 for the 90-degree ejection angle to 573,087 × 10^5 for the 0-degree ejection angle, indicating a transition to turbulent flow.
The RCS of the non-turbulent chaff cloud at 100 milliseconds was similar to the RCS of the turbulent chaff cloud at 50 milliseconds.

The study shows that turbulence plays a crucial role in the rapid blooming and RCS development of chaff clouds, which is important for the effective deception of radar-guided missiles in the initial stages of engagement.
The findings can be extrapolated to simulate the effect of turbulence on practical chaff cartridges consisting of millions of filaments.
Chaff is based on the expulsion of numerous electrical dipoles of different lengths to cover a broad spectrum of radar frequencies, helping to deceive enemy missiles.
The dynamic RCS of a target is the measure of the backscattered power per unit solid angle respective to the incident power, and it varies with the frequency and target aspect.
The blooming of a chaff cloud is crucial for achieving the required RCS to effectively deceive radar-guided missiles.
Turbulence can enhance the efficiency of the chaff cartridge in the initial engagement and effective break lock of the missile.
